responses.reason: S2 just says share gains in the independent restaurant channel drove the $507,000 increase, but there is no customer count, channel split, or contract data anywhere in the memo backing that up, only the sentence itself, so I would want a channel breakdown before relying on it.

Three freight invoices worth $31,200 relate to August shipments but get posted to September because the vendor portal closed early, so account 5100 is missing part of what it should show for August and the period does not match when the cost was actually incurred.

Recomputing unrounded, July's margin was about 23.5 percent and August's was about 21.9 percent, so the claim that margin held flat at 22 percent in both months does not survive, margin actually compressed by more than a point and the conclusion in S1 does not hold.

S10 says no new legal matters arose in August, and S11 describes the same $185,000 accrual as a new claim notified to the broker in August, both cannot be true, and I would believe S11 since it is the one tied to an actual dollar entry posted this month.

S9 describes releasing a July trade show accrual into August expense ahead of a September show, which reads like the cost is tied to whichever period the accrual happens to move in rather than the month the show actually happens, so the right period is not clear from the sentence.

Warehouse wages fell $37,700 while temporary labor rose $86,800 in the same month, so total labor cost across the two lines actually went up about $49,100, which cuts against calling the wage decline a pure productivity gain, and neither sentence acknowledges the other account at all.

Supplier rebates jumped $172,000, a 409.5 percent move that clears both threshold legs by a wide margin, and none of the twelve sentences in the memo mention this account, so it cannot go out without someone explaining what drove the rebate increase.

S7 already gives a specific reason for the flat balance, straight line amortization out to a named date in March 2027 with no endorsement issued, and that is concrete enough that I would not flag a zero variance just because it happens to be exactly zero.

Repairs only moved $8,400, which fails the dollar leg of the threshold even though the percent is high, and the rule stated at the top needs both legs to clear, so no driver was actually required here.

The table shows service revenue fell $111,000, from $1,096,000 down to $985,000, but S3 says it grew by that same amount, so the sentence has the direction exactly backwards from what the account actually did.

My table for this case only runs July against August for fleet fuel, there is no June column in it, so I cannot verify a $91,200 June figure or confirm a repeated cutoff problem from what I have in front of me here.

Bad debt only moved $1,700, which fails the dollar leg of the threshold by a wide margin, so Sentence S6 was never required, and three clauses of detail on a trivial line may have taken space from something that actually needed an explanation, like the supplier rebate account.

S12 leans on the same productivity program already used to explain the $37,700 wage decline, but a program that affects labor hours does not automatically explain a $44,800 change in inventory shrink, and nothing in the memo ties the program specifically to shrink counts.
